extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers, conference authors, and the peer-review community (particularly NeurIPS authors/organizers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and evaluating how authors' self-assessed acceptance probabilities and paper-rankings (at submission and after reviews) compare to co-authors' judgments and peer-review outcomes for NeurIPS 2021 submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q1: Authors' estimated probability of acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time of paper submission, authors were asked: 'What is your best estimate of the probability (as a percentage) that this submission will be accepted?'. This captures each author's perceived likelihood of acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors were informed of historical acceptance rates (~21%); NeurIPS 2021 acceptance was 25.8%. Authors greatly overestimated: median prediction was 70%. Use reported percentages to compare perceived vs actual acceptance rates and to measure overconfidence/overestimation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration error of authors' predictions (Brier score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how well authors' predicted acceptance probabilities match actual outcomes, quantified using the Brier score (squared loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute Brier scores and control for confounders to compare calibration across sub-groups. Findings: female authors had slightly but statistically significantly higher calibration error than male authors; miscalibration decreased with seniority; invited (meta-)reviewers were better calibrated. All examined sub-groups over-predicted acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q2: Authors' internal ranking of multiple submissions by perceived scientific contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: For authors submitting two or more papers, they were asked to 'Rank your submissions in terms of your own perception of their scientific contributions to the NeurIPS community, if published in their current form.' This captures internal relative judgments of quality among an author's own papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strict rankings provided by authors to compare perceived scientific merit among an author's submissions. In the data, strict rankings from Q2 agreed with rankings induced by Q1 predicted acceptance probabilities for 93% of responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between perceived merit ranking (Q2) and predicted acceptance (Q1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement between the strict ranking of submissions by perceived scientific merit (Q2) and the strict ranking induced by predicted acceptance probabilities (Q1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure percent agreement: the study found 93% agreement, but noted ~7% of cases where authors thought the peer review was more likely to reject the paper they judged better. Use this metric to detect mismatches between perceived scientific value and expectation of reviewer behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-author agreement on relative quality of joint papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which co-authors agree with each other when ranking the relative scientific contribution of papers they co-authored (from Q2 responses provided by multiple co-authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare pairwise rankings from overlapping-authors samples. Findings: co-authors disagreed about a third of the time — similar in magnitude to author-reviewer disagreements. In pairs where one paper was accepted and another rejected, authors rated the rejected paper higher about one-third of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q3: Change in authors' perception after reading preliminary reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading preliminary reviews, authors were asked how their perception of the paper's scientific contribution changed, using a five-point multiple-choice scale: much more positive ('++'), slightly more positive ('+'), did not change ('0'), slightly more negative ('-'), much more negative ('--').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate responses to measure the impact of reviews on author perception. The study found that about 50% of authors reported a change in perception after seeing initial reviews, and over 30% reported becoming more positive (applies to both accepted and rejected papers). Use distribution over the five categories to quantify review influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' ability to predict relative acceptance outcomes among their own papers
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing two papers from the same author, whether the author correctly predicts which will be accepted (or which has higher acceptance probability), especially in cases where one was eventually accepted and the other rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure frequency of cases where an author rated the rejected paper higher than the accepted one. The study observed that in such mixed-outcome pairs authors rated the rejected paper higher roughly one-third of the time, indicating limited predictive accuracy in relative judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overestimation / overconfidence bias in authors' acceptance forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic tendency of authors to overestimate their chances of acceptance relative to actual acceptance rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare central tendency of authors' predicted probabilities to historical and actual acceptance rates. The paper reports nearly three-fold overestimate (median 70% vs actual ~25.8%), suggesting organizers/mentors should attempt to recalibrate expectations prior to conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication: noisiness and subjectivity of paper-quality assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that disagreement exists not only among reviewers but also among authors and co-authors, implying that assessing paper quality is a noisy and potentially fundamentally subjective task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the documented disagreement rates (author-reviewer, co-author, inter-reviewer from complementary experiments) to argue for caution in interpreting accept/reject outcomes and to inform policy discussions (e.g., acceptance policies, emphasis on technical correctness vs subjective significance). This is a conceptual criterion rather than a numeric score.
